seo.title: How to Create a Google Business Profile (2026)
seo.meta_description: How to create a Google Business Profile for an Anaheim or Orange County business: eligibility, Google Account, adding your business and verification.

h1: How to Create a Google Business Profile: Step by Step for Local Businesses
answer: To create a Google Business Profile, sign in with a Google Account, go to business.google.com/add, add your business details and complete verification. It is free. Google says profiles are for businesses that meet customers in person, at a storefront or at the customer's location, not online-only businesses. For Anaheim and Orange County businesses it is the first step in local search.
key_takeaways: Only businesses that meet customers in person qualify.
Search for an existing profile before creating one.

sections.heading: What a Business Profile does
sections.body_html: Google's help page says a Business Profile lets you manage how your business shows up on Maps and Search at no charge. You can keep hours, website, phone number and location accurate, post photos and videos, collect and respond to reviews, and direct customers to your website, social media and booking links. For a business in Anaheim or anywhere in Orange County, it is usually the first thing a nearby customer sees.

sections.heading: Check you're eligible
sections.body_html: Google says Business Profiles suit businesses that interact with customers in person during business hours, such as retail stores and service providers that visit customers. They are not for online-only businesses or for properties for rent or sale. Google states that only businesses making face-to-face contact with customers are eligible; online-only businesses are pointed to Google Ads instead.

sections.heading: Storefront or service area
sections.body_html: Depending on your category, your location can be a street address, a service area or a place marker. A shop or office that customers visit uses its address. A plumber or cleaner who visits customers sets a service area and hides the home address.

sections.heading: Get a Google Account ready
sections.body_html: You need a Google Account to sign up. Google says you can create one with a Gmail address or your preferred email, or use an existing account with any email address. It suggests linking a company email to make management easier. Use an account the business controls, not one tied to a single employee.

sections.heading: Search for an existing profile first
sections.body_html: Many businesses already have a profile created from public information. Search for your business name and city on Google Maps. If it exists and is unverified, claim it instead of creating a duplicate.

sections.heading: Add your business
sections.body_html: Google's steps: go to business.google.com/add, select Add your business to Google, follow the on-screen instructions to add your details, then select a verification option. Google stresses that your address must be correct and meet its guidelines.

sections.heading: Choose the right name and category
sections.body_html: Use your real-world business name exactly as it appears on your signage and paperwork, without added keywords, and the most specific primary category. These two choices affect which searches you appear in and whether the profile stays in good standing.

sections.heading: Verify the profile
sections.body_html: Verification proves you own the business. Google decides which methods you can use, such as phone, email, video or postcard. Until you verify, you cannot fully manage the profile.

sections.heading: Multiple locations
sections.body_html: Google says larger businesses with multiple locations can use the Business Profile Manager to manage profiles in bulk. Each real location gets its own profile; do not create profiles for places you do not operate.

sections.heading: After you're verified
sections.body_html: Complete everything: hours, services, attributes, photos and a description. Then build the habits that keep it strong: asking every customer for a review, replying to reviews and updating details when they change.

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.body_html:
• Business meets customers in person.
  • Google Account the business controls.
  • Searched Maps for an existing profile.
  • Real-world name, no added keywords.
  • Specific primary category.
  • Correct address or service area.
  • Verification completed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes when creating a profile
sections.body_html:
• Creating a new profile when one already exists, which splits reviews and confuses customers.
  • Adding city names or service keywords to the business name to try to rank higher.
  • Listing a home address that customers never visit instead of setting a service area.
  • Using a personal Gmail tied to one employee, so the business loses access when they leave.
  • Choosing a broad primary category such as Contractor when a specific one such as Roofing contractor fits.
  • Leaving the profile half-finished after verification, with no hours, services or photos.

sections.heading: What to prepare before you start
sections.body_html: Gather everything in one place before you sign in: the exact business name from your signage or paperwork, the address or the list of cities you serve, a phone number answered during business hours, your website address, opening hours, a short description of what you do, and a handful of real photos of your premises, team or work. Decide who will own the profile and who will help manage it. Having this ready turns a frustrating afternoon into a fifteen-minute task, and it means the details Google shows from day one are complete and consistent with your website. For a new business in Anaheim, Fullerton, Irvine or anywhere else in Orange County, that first impression on Maps often decides whether a nearby customer calls you or the business next to you.

sections.heading: An example
sections.body_html: Imagine a new dog grooming business in Fullerton that visits clients in a van. The owner signs in with the business Google Account, searches Maps and finds no existing profile, then adds the business at business.google.com/add. Because the groomer travels to customers, the profile uses a service area instead of the owner's home address. After verifying by video, the owner adds services, photos of the van and real grooming results, and starts asking every client for a review.

sections.heading: How this fits your local plan
sections.body_html: This task is one piece of a wider local plan. Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, so the profile, your website and your reputation all have to agree. A practical order for most Orange County businesses is: get the Business Profile verified and accurate, make the name, address and phone identical everywhere, publish one clear page per service, then build a steady habit of genuine reviews and replies. Each step makes the next one work better, and the same signals help AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI features describe your business correctly when someone in Anaheim asks for a recommendation.

sections.heading: Questions owners ask us
sections.body_html: Owners often ask how long it takes before a new profile appears in searches. Once it is verified and complete, it can start showing for searches near you, but visibility grows with time, reviews and accurate details rather than overnight. Another common question is whether a business with no storefront can still have a profile; it can, as long as it meets customers in person at their location, using a service area. Finally, owners ask whether they should create profiles for nearby cities they serve. They should not: one real business location gets one profile, and the service area tells Google which cities you cover.

sections.heading: What to do this week
sections.body_html:
1. Search Maps for your business.
  2. Confirm which Google Account will own it.
  3. Add or claim the profile.
  4. Start verification.

sections.heading: When to get help
sections.body_html: Most of this can be done in-house with an hour or two and careful reading of Google's own help pages. It is worth bringing in help when the stakes are high or the problem keeps coming back: a profile that has been suspended more than once, many locations to manage, a site that keeps failing the same checks, or no time to keep up the routine. A good local SEO partner should explain what they will change and why, point to Google's guidelines rather than promise rankings, and leave you with access to every account. sections.heading: The short version
sections.body_html: Check eligibility, search for an existing profile, add your business at business.google.com/add with an accurate name, category and address, then verify. Chimera, based in Anaheim, helps Orange County businesses set this up correctly the first time.

faqs.q: Is a Google Business Profile free?
faqs.a: Yes. Google says you can manage your profile on Maps and Search at no charge.

faqs.q: Can an online-only business have a Business Profile?
faqs.a: No. Google says only businesses that make face-to-face contact with customers are eligible.

faqs.q: Where do I create a Business Profile?
faqs.a: At business.google.com/add, signed in to a Google Account.

faqs.q: What if my business is already on Google?
faqs.a: Claim the existing profile instead of creating a new one.

faqs.q: Do I need a Gmail address?
faqs.a: No. Google says you can use your preferred email address for the Google Account.

faqs.q: How do businesses with many locations manage profiles?
faqs.a: Google points them to the Business Profile Manager for bulk management.
